# R01 — React fundamentals and internal mechanics React 18 unless a question says otherwise. Questions REACT-001–REACT-050. Covers function components, props, JSX, elements vs fibers, state and batching, reconciliation and keys, render/commit, concurrent scheduling, context, roots/hydration, controlled inputs, refs, portals, and purity mistakes that corrupt state. ### REACT-001 — A function component is a render function **Difficulty:** Intermediate **Category:** Components **Question:** What does React treat a function component as? When does React call it, and what is the return value for? **Answer:** React treats a function component as a plain function that takes props and hook state and returns a description of the UI. React calls it during the render phase, when it needs to know what that part of the screen should look like. The return value is a tree of React elements (or `null`, a string, a number, or an array), not the DOM itself. React compares it with the previous description and updates the real DOM later, in the commit phase. Keep it pure, since React may call it more than once. **Code:** ```tsx function Greeting({ name }: { name: string }) { return name ?

Hello {name}

: null; } ``` **Follow-up:** Why does Strict Mode call the component twice in development, and does production do that? Answer: It is a development-only check that helps you spot impure code, and only one result is committed. Production does not add that extra call. Concurrent rendering can still repeat or throw away a render in production when it needs to reschedule work. ### REACT-002 — Props are owned by the parent **Difficulty:** Intermediate **Category:** Props **Question:** Who owns a prop value? What happens if the child writes `props.title = "Edited"`, or if it does `const [title, setTitle] = useState(props.title)` and the parent later passes a new title? **Answer:** The parent owns a prop. The child only reads it on each render. If the child tries to assign `props.title`, React throws an error in development because props are frozen, and the parent never sees the change. Mutating a nested object inside props can still leak back, so avoid that too. `useState(props.title)` only uses the prop as the starting value. When the parent later passes a new title, the state keeps the old one until you call `setTitle` or remount the component with a different `key`. Use that pattern only when the prop is meant to be an initial value. **Code:** ```tsx function Field({ title }: { title: string }) { const [draft, setDraft] = useState(title); // stays at first title return setDraft(e.target.value)} />; } ``` **Trade-offs:** Controlled `value`/`onChange` when the parent must see every change; keyed remount when a new entity should discard the draft. **Follow-up:** When is storing a prop in state a real API, rather than a stale copy? Answer: When the prop is clearly documented as an initial value, like `defaultValue`. If callers need live updates, make the component controlled with `value` and `onChange`, or change its `key` to reset it. ### REACT-003 — JSX is an element description **Difficulty:** Intermediate **Category:** JSX **Question:** What does `` compile to, why must `Profile` be capitalized, and what does React do with `{user.name}`, `false`, `0`, and a plain object as a child? **Answer:** JSX compiles to a call to `jsx` (or `createElement` in the older setup). That call returns a plain object with a `type`, `props`, and `key`. It does not run the component and it does not touch the DOM. The capital letter tells the compiler that `Profile` is a variable pointing to your component. A lowercase name would be treated as a built-in HTML tag. As children, strings and numbers become text. `null`, `undefined`, and `false` render nothing. `0` renders the text "0". A plain object is not a valid child and throws. **Follow-up:** What is the difference between an element and a component? Answer: The component is the function or class you wrote. The element is a small object, `{ type, props, key }`, that points at it. React only runs the component when it renders that element at a spot in the tree, not when the object is created. ### REACT-004 — Elements, fibers, and DOM nodes **Difficulty:** Senior **Category:** Elements **Question:** Define a component, a React element, a fiber, and a DOM node. Which one holds hook state? If the module creates `const element = ` once and two different parents return that same object, do those parents share Counter state? **Answer:** A component is the function you write. An element is a lightweight description of what to render, created on every render. A fiber is React's internal record for one mounted instance of something in the tree. A DOM node is the real browser object created during commit. Hook state lives on the fiber, not on the element. If two parents return the same element object, React still creates two separate fibers. Each gets its own state. They only share the same props reference. So reusing an element is not the same as sharing an instance. **Trade-offs:** Hoist a constant element only when it never closes over changing data. Shared state needs a common parent or external store—not a shared element object. **Follow-up:** Does a parent re-render that returns `` again destroy Counter's state? Answer: No. As long as the type and key at that position are the same, React reuses the existing fiber and keeps its state. State is lost only when the type or key changes, or when that position is removed. ### REACT-005 — setState schedules the next render **Difficulty:** Intermediate **Category:** State **Question:** ```tsx function onClick() { setCount(count + 1); console.log(count); } ``` `count` is `0` in this render. What does the log print, when does the component function run again, and what does the screen show relative to the `setCount` line? **Answer:** The log prints `0`. The handler closed over the `count` from the render that created it, and `setCount` does not change that variable. It only schedules a new render. For a discrete click on a `createRoot` app, React finishes your handler first, then runs the component again with `count` as `1`, and updates the DOM before the browser paints. So on the very next line, both your variable and the screen still show the old value. The new value only exists in the next render. **Follow-up:** `useState(expensive())` versus `useState(() => expensive())` — what runs on the second render? Answer: With `useState(expensive())`, the call happens on every render, but React ignores the result after the first one. With the function form, React calls the initializer only when it creates the state, not on later renders. In development Strict Mode, it may call it twice on mount. ### REACT-006 — useState replaces object state **Difficulty:** Intermediate **Category:** State **Question:** A component holds `useState({ a: 1, b: 2 })` and calls `setPair({ a: 3 })`. What is `b` on the next render? How does that differ from class `this.setState({ a: 3 })`? **Answer:** After `setPair({ a: 3 })`, the state is just `{ a: 3 }`, and `b` is gone. A `useState` setter replaces the whole value. A class `this.setState` merges the new keys into the old state, so `b` would have stayed. With hooks, you do the merge yourself using an updater that spreads the previous object. That spread only copies one level deep. Also, a new object always counts as a change, even when the fields look the same, so React will re-render. Other `useState` slots in the component are not affected. **Code:** ```tsx setPair((prev) => ({ ...prev, a: 3 })); // { a: 3, b: 2 } ``` **Follow-up:** What does React guarantee about the identity of the `setPair` function across renders? Answer: The setter keeps the same identity for the life of that state, so you can safely leave it out of dependency arrays. That stability only applies to the function. The state value itself still changes. ### REACT-007 — Updates in one batch run in order **Difficulty:** Senior **Category:** State **Question:** `count` is `5`. Three click handlers: `plain` does `setCount(count + 1)` twice; `functional` does `setCount(c => c + 1)` twice; `mixed` does updater, then `setCount(count + 1)`, then updater. What is `count` after each? **Answer:** React queues updates and applies them in order on the next render. A plain value replaces whatever result is pending. An updater function receives the pending result and returns the next one. `plain` ends at `6`, because both calls compute from the same `5`. `functional` ends at `7`, because the second updater starts from `6`. `mixed` goes to `6` with the first updater, then the plain value `count + 1` replaces it with `6` again, and the last updater makes it `7`. Plain values use this render's snapshot. Updaters use the pending state. **Follow-up:** If `mixed` used two different slots, does one see the other's pending value? Answer: No. Each state slot has its own queue. They are processed in the same batch and commit together, but one does not feed into the other. If one value depends on another, derive it during render. ### REACT-008 — React 18 batches outside React events **Difficulty:** Senior **Category:** Batching **Question:** In one callback, `setCount` and `setFlag` both run. Compare a React `onClick`, `setTimeout`, `fetch().then`, and a native `addEventListener` click on React 18 `createRoot` versus React 17. **Answer:** Batching means React groups several state updates into one render. In React 18 with `createRoot`, that happens everywhere: React event handlers, timeouts, promise callbacks, and native listeners. Both updates apply, then React renders and commits once. In React 17, batching only worked inside React's own event handlers. The same pair in a timeout, a promise, or a native listener caused two renders. The old `ReactDOM.render` API keeps that React 17 behavior. Batching does not change variables you already read. Those still hold the old values. **Code:** ```tsx setTimeout(() => { setCount((c) => c + 1); setFlag((f) => !f); }, 0); // createRoot: one render ``` **Follow-up:** A click calls `setQuery(next)` and, inside `startTransition`, `setResults(...)`. Still one render? Answer: No. Batching only groups updates with the same priority. The urgent update and the transition can render and commit separately, and the transition can be interrupted. ### REACT-009 — An await starts a new batch **Difficulty:** Advanced **Category:** Batching **Question:** ```tsx async function onClick() { setA(1); setB(2); await save(); setA(3); setB(4); } ``` How many renders on React 18 `createRoot` if `save` resolves? On React 17? What if you remove the `await`? **Answer:** In React 18 with `createRoot`, you get two renders. The two updates before `await` are batched into one render. After the promise resolves, the code continues in a separate task, and those two updates are batched into a second render. In React 17, you get three. The first pair is batched because it is inside the event handler, but after the `await`, each setter renders on its own. If you remove the `await`, all four calls form one batch. The last values win, so the screen goes straight to `a=3` and `b=4`, and `(1, 2)` is never painted. **Follow-up:** `save` rejects before the second pair. What has the user seen? Answer: The first batch has already committed, so the user saw `(1, 2)`. Handle the error in a `catch` and set an error state. A clear status field is better than leaving a half-finished "saving" screen. ### REACT-010 — flushSync commits before it returns **Difficulty:** Advanced **Category:** Batching **Question:** A click appends a row and must read that row's `getBoundingClientRect()` before later logic in the same handler. What does `flushSync` change about batching and commit, and what about the `count` binding? **Answer:** `flushSync` tells React to process the updates inside its callback right now. React renders and commits them before `flushSync` returns, so the DOM is already updated when the next line runs. That lets you measure the new row immediately. Updates outside the callback still follow the normal batching path. Variables from the current render, like `count`, do not change. The newer render inside `flushSync` has its own variables. It blocks the main thread, so use it only when the next imperative line truly needs the updated DOM. **Code:** ```tsx flushSync(() => setRows((rows) => [...rows, nextRow])); const height = listRef.current?.lastElementChild?.getBoundingClientRect().height; ``` **Trade-offs:** Prefer `useLayoutEffect` when measurement can live with every commit. Prefer deriving position from state when possible. **Follow-up:** `flushSync` appends a row, then `setSavedAt` outside. One commit? Answer: No. The append commits inside `flushSync`, and `setSavedAt` is a separate, later update. If both must appear in the same commit, put both inside the same `flushSync` callback. ### REACT-011 — Reconciliation matches type at a position **Difficulty:** Senior **Category:** Reconciliation **Question:** A parent renders `
` then `
` with no keys. Does React move instances? What happens to state? Why this heuristic? **Answer:** Reconciliation is how React decides whether to reuse or replace what is already on screen. Without keys, React compares siblings by position. At position 0, the type changed from `UserCard` to `Details`, so React unmounts the old one and mounts a new one. The same happens at position 1, and state and effects reset. React does not search the siblings for a matching type to move. If the type and key at a position are the same, React keeps the instance and updates its props. This rule is simple and fast. Keys exist for lists where order can change. **Follow-up:** Why does declaring `function UserCard` inside the parent reset state every parent render? Answer: React compares component types by reference. A function declared inside the parent is a brand new function each render, so React sees a different type and remounts it. Define components at module level so the reference stays stable. ### REACT-012 — Index keys work while order is identity **Difficulty:** Senior **Category:** Keys **Question:** A todo list uses `key={index}`; rows hold draft state and uncontrolled inputs. When is that correct, and what breaks on insert-at-front or sort? What should the key be? **Answer:** A key tells React which item a row represents. An index key means "the item in this position," which is fine only when the list is static and rows have no state of their own. If you insert at the front or sort, the item at each index changes. React reuses the row at that index with new props, but keeps the old draft state and input text, so typed text ends up next to the wrong item. Use a stable id like `todo.id`. Keys must be unique among siblings, and random keys remount every row on every render. **Code:** ```tsx {todos.map((todo) => ( ))} ``` **Follow-up:** Filtered list keyed by `todo.id`—do surviving rows keep drafts? Answer: Yes. Rows with matching keys keep their instances and state. With index keys, a filtered list would shift drafts onto the wrong items. ### REACT-013 — State stays where type and key stay **Difficulty:** Senior **Category:** State preservation **Question:** For each: `{isUser ? : }`, `{isUser ? : }`, `{isUser ? : }`, `{isUser ? : }`—does Panel state survive toggling `isUser`? **Answer:** React keeps state as long as the component type, key, and position stay the same. In the first case, both branches render `Panel` at the same position, so state survives. In the second, the type changes from `UserPanel` to `GuestPanel`, so React remounts and state resets. In the third, the type is the same and only a prop changes, so state survives. You must read `kind` from props, or reset on purpose. In the fourth, the key changes, which forces a remount. That is the supported way to reset state. **Code:** ```tsx ``` **Follow-up:** Key changes on `Panel` which renders a `textarea` with its own `useState`. Does the textarea keep text? Answer: No. Changing the key remounts `Panel` and everything inside it, including local state and focus. If some state must survive, lift it above the keyed component. ### REACT-014 — Two conditional slots are two positions **Difficulty:** Senior **Category:** State preservation **Question:** `Editor` drafts from `doc.text`. Compare ternary switching `docA`/`docB`, two `&&` editors, and one `` when switching A→B→A. **Answer:** With the ternary or the single ``, there is only one position, so React keeps the same instance. The draft was initialized from A, so it stays even after the props describe B. With two `&&` editors, there are two separate positions. Switching unmounts one and mounts the other. When you return to A, it re-reads `docA.text`, and whatever you typed is gone. To remount per document, use `key={doc.id}`. To keep drafts, lift a map of drafts by id above the switch. **Code:** ```tsx ``` **Trade-offs:** CSS-hidden dual editors keep both drafts (and effects). Parent `Record` keeps drafts without a hidden tree. **Follow-up:** `Editor` moves from under `TabPanelA` to under `TabPanelB`. Does the draft move? Answer: No. State belongs to the instance at a specific place in the tree. Moving it under a different parent destroys the old instance and creates a new one. Lift the state above both panels if it must survive. ### REACT-015 — Render describes, commit applies **Difficulty:** Senior **Category:** Render and commit **Question:** What work is render vs commit? Which phase can run for an update the user never sees? Where do a layout DOM read and a subscription belong? **Answer:** React works in two phases. In the render phase, it calls your components and works out what changed. It does not touch the DOM. In the commit phase, it applies the changes to the DOM, attaches refs, and runs effects. Render can be paused, restarted, or thrown away in concurrent mode, so the user may never see some render passes. Commit runs to completion without interruption. Put subscriptions in `useEffect` or event handlers. Put layout reads and writes that must happen before the browser paints in `useLayoutEffect`. Keep the component body pure. **Follow-up:** `useLayoutEffect` calls `setState`. Does the user see the first committed tree? Answer: No. React runs that update synchronously before the browser paints. If you did the same `setState` in `useEffect`, the browser could paint the in-between state first. ### REACT-016 — A fiber is the unit of work **Difficulty:** Advanced **Category:** Fiber **Question:** What is a fiber vs a JSX element? Why replace the stack reconciler? What is `alternate` for? **Answer:** A fiber is React's internal object for one piece of the UI. It stores things like the component type, props, hook state, and links to its parent, child, and sibling. A JSX element is just a cheap description created on each render. The old stack-based reconciler had to finish a whole tree walk in one go. Fibers break that into small units, so React can pause, resume, or abandon work. React keeps a current fiber tree and a work-in-progress copy, linked by `alternate`. When the new tree is ready, commit swaps them. **Follow-up:** If render writes only work-in-progress, how can an impure render still corrupt the screen? Answer: An impure render can write to places outside the work-in-progress tree, like module variables, stores, or shared objects. Throwing away the work-in-progress tree does not undo those writes. Keeping render pure is what makes it safe to discard. ### REACT-017 — Render can yield; commit runs through **Difficulty:** Advanced **Category:** Fiber **Question:** Under concurrent rendering, a transition render is in progress and the user clicks. What happens to the in-progress render? Mid-commit? Do effect cleanups run for a thrown-away render? **Answer:** While a transition render is in progress, React can pause it and handle the urgent click first. It may then throw away the partial work and start over later. The screen keeps showing the last committed result. Once React starts a commit, it does not yield. DOM updates, refs, and layout effects finish in one go. A discarded render never reached commit, so its effects never ran, and there is nothing to clean up. But anything you started inside the component body, like a fetch, has no cleanup. That is another reason to keep render pure. **Follow-up:** Why does Strict Mode remount effects on mount if discarded renders never run effects? Answer: It is a separate mechanism. In development, Strict Mode mounts, cleans up, and mounts again, to catch missing cleanups. It has nothing to do with the scheduler abandoning work. Production mounts once. ### REACT-018 — Transitions keep the keystroke urgent **Difficulty:** Senior **Category:** Scheduling **Question:** A controlled input updates `query` and filters a huge table from the same update; typing stalls. How keep input urgent and table interruptible? What do you give up? What does this not speed up? **Answer:** Keep `setQuery` as a normal urgent update so the input responds immediately. Mark the table update as a transition with `startTransition`, or pass `useDeferredValue(query)` to the heavy child. React can then show the typed text first and render the table in the background, interrupting it if you type again. The trade-off is that the table briefly lags behind the input, so you may show a pending state. This does not make the filtering itself faster, does not reduce network requests, and does not fix rendering 20,000 rows. Use windowing for that. **Code:** ```tsx const [query, setQuery] = useState(""); const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query); // input uses query; Table uses deferredQuery ``` **Follow-up:** How does `useDeferredValue` differ from copying in `useEffect`? Answer: Copying in an effect triggers a second normal-priority render after paint. A deferred value is scheduled as a transition, so it can be interrupted by the next keystroke. ### REACT-019 — Lanes are the internal priority model **Difficulty:** Staff-Level **Category:** Scheduling **Question:** What is a lane in React 18 at a level you can defend: what an update carries, how render chooses work, how urgent vs transition interact, and what is public API? **Answer:** A lane is React's internal way of labeling how urgent an update is. Each update gets a lane when it is scheduled. When React renders, it picks which lanes to process now and leaves the others queued. That is how a click can commit while a transition is abandoned: discrete input has a higher priority than transitions. Expiration rules stop low-priority work from starving. Lanes are an internal detail, not public API. In app code you use `startTransition`, `useTransition`, `useDeferredValue`, and `useSyncExternalStore`. Updates in the same lane are still batched together. **Follow-up:** Why can an external store tear, and what does `useSyncExternalStore` change? Answer: With interruptible rendering, different components can read different versions of a store across passes. `useSyncExternalStore` checks the snapshot again and forces a synchronous re-render if it changed, so the commit stays consistent. Cache the snapshot, or a new object each call looks like a constant change. ### REACT-020 — A parent render runs child functions **Difficulty:** Intermediate **Category:** Rendering **Question:** Parent state changes. `Child` gets the same primitive props, no state, no `memo`. Does Child run? Is the DOM rewritten? What to change first if the profiler is hot? **Answer:** Yes, `Child` runs again. When the parent renders, it creates new child elements, and React calls the child component even if its props look identical. Without `memo`, equal props alone do not skip the call. The DOM is not rebuilt, though. React only updates DOM nodes whose output actually changed. So the cost is in JavaScript and reconciliation, not in rewriting the page. If the profiler shows this is hot, restructure first: move the changing state into a smaller component so the expensive siblings are not affected. Use `memo` only after measuring. **Trade-offs:** Default re-render until measured. State colocation beats blanket `memo`/`useCallback`. New object/callback props defeat `memo`. **Follow-up:** `memo(Child)` also uses `useContext(ThemeContext)`. Provider value changes, props unchanged. Skip? Answer: No. `memo` only compares props, and context is not a prop. A component that reads a context still re-renders when that context's value changes. ### REACT-021 — Hook identity is call order **Difficulty:** Intermediate **Category:** Components **Question:** Why does this throw when `enabled` becomes `false` after a true first render? ```tsx function Panel({ enabled }: { enabled: boolean }) { if (!enabled) return null; const [open, setOpen] = useState(false); return ; } ``` **Answer:** React doesn't track hooks by name. It stores them as an ordered list on the component and matches each call by its position. On the first render, `useState` was call number one. On the second render, the component returns early before reaching `useState`, so React finds fewer hooks than last time and throws an error. Returning `null` early is fine for the UI. It is not fine for hooks. Always call every hook first, then decide what to return. **Code:** ```tsx function Panel({ enabled }: { enabled: boolean }) { const [open, setOpen] = useState(false); if (!enabled) return null; return ; } ``` **Follow-up:** Conditional `useAuth()` that itself calls three hooks—what breaks? Answer: Those three hook slots appear and disappear in the caller's list, which breaks the order. This is the same violation as a conditional `useState`. Always call custom hooks unconditionally. ### REACT-022 — The timeout closes over the render that scheduled it **Difficulty:** Senior **Category:** State **Question:** Three clicks within 500ms each schedule `setTimeout(() => { console.log(count); setCount(count + 1); }, 500)` with `count` starting at `0`. What logs and what is final `count`? **Answer:** Each click runs a handler created in a render where `count` is `0`. The handler only starts a timer. It does not update state, so nothing re-renders between the clicks, and all three timers capture `0`. When they fire, each logs `0` and calls `setCount(1)`. The first sets it to `1`. The next two set the same value, so React bails out. The final count is `1`, not `3`. If you use `setCount(c => c + 1)`, the final count is `3`, because the updater uses the latest state. The log still prints `0`. **Code:** ```tsx setTimeout(() => { console.log(count); // closed-over snapshot setCount((c) => c + 1); }, 500); ``` **Follow-up:** Functional updater + `console.log(count)` after the same three overlapping clicks? Answer: You get three logs of `0` and a final count of `3`. The log reads the stale variable from the closure, while the updater works with the latest state. ### REACT-023 — Same state skips the render **Difficulty:** Intermediate **Category:** State **Question:** `count` is `0` and handler calls `setCount(0)`. Object state: `setPair({ n: 0 })` vs mutate then `setPair(pair)`? **Answer:** When you set state, React compares the new value with the current one using `Object.is`. If they are equal, it skips the re-render. So `setCount(0)` when the count is already `0` does nothing visible. `setPair({ n: 0 })` creates a new object with a different reference. React treats it as changed and re-renders. It does not compare fields deeply. If you mutate `pair.n` and call `setPair(pair)`, the reference is unchanged. React skips the update, but the object was already changed, so the screen can go stale. Return `prev` from an updater when nothing changed. **Follow-up:** `setCount(c => c)` when `c` is `0`? Updater returns `{ ...c }` for object state? Answer: Returning the same value bails out. Returning a copy, even with the same fields, is a new reference, so React re-renders. ### REACT-024 — The key has to sit on the sibling **Difficulty:** Advanced **Category:** Reconciliation **Question:** Mapping items to `<>
…
…
` inside a `
`—what is wrong when the list reorders and rows will hold state? Why not wrap in a `
`? **Answer:** The key must be on the element that the `map` returns, because that is what React compares among siblings. Here the shorthand `<>` fragment cannot take a key. The `key` on `dt` only identifies children inside the fragment, not the fragments themselves. So the fragments are matched by index. After a reorder, state sticks to the position instead of the item. The fix is ``. Wrapping with a `
` would give a key, but it breaks the valid structure of a `
` and hurts accessibility. **Code:** ```tsx {items.map((item) => (
{item.term}
{item.def}
 ))} ``` **Follow-up:** Why can `` take a key when `<>` cannot? Answer: The `<>` shorthand has no way to pass props, so it cannot carry a key. The explicit `Fragment` accepts `key` like any element, and React then treats it as a normal keyed sibling. ### REACT-025 — The draft followed the index, not the id **Difficulty:** Staff-Level **Category:** State preservation **Question:** Fifty `Line` rows use `useState(item.amount)` and `key={index}`. After blur, parent batches `setLines(payload.lines)` (reordered) and `setSavedAt`. Typed draft for id `"L3"` appears on another id. Why? How keep draft with `"L3"`? How force server amount instead? **Answer:** Keys decide which instance belongs to which item. With `key={index}`, the row at position 2 keeps its instance and its draft state, even though a different item now sits there after the reorder. `useState(item.amount)` only reads the prop once, so it never picks up the new item. Fix it with `key={item.id}`, so each draft follows its item. To force the server amount into the draft, adjust state during render when `item.amount` changes, with a guard so it settles. Or remount using a versioned key, which also drops focus. **Code:** ```tsx {lines.map((item) => ( ))} ``` **Follow-up:** Id-keyed fiber still shows typed draft after server amount change. Why, and how paint server amount before paint without remounting? Answer: The type and key matched, so React preserved the state, including the old draft. To show the server amount without remounting, compare the incoming amount with a stored copy and set the draft during render. React restarts the render before painting. Adding the amount to the key works too, but it remounts. ### REACT-026 — `children` is an element the parent already created **Difficulty:** Intermediate **Category:** Props **Question:** `` with `{children}` inside `Card`. Who creates `Counter`, when does it run, where is state? Difference of `{children}`, `{children()}`, ``? **Answer:** The component that writes `` creates the `Counter` element during its own render. That is only a description, so `Counter` has not run yet. `Card` places it in its output, and React then renders `Counter` at that spot. Its state lives there. `{children}` renders the element that was passed in. `{children()}` only works if the parent passed a function, and that function must stay pure. `` treats `children` as a component type, which is wrong for an element object, and a new function each render would remount. **Follow-up:** `Card` renders `{children}` in two sibling slots. Shared state? Shared ref? Answer: No. React creates two separate instances, each with its own state. They share only the element object. A single ref cannot attach to both. ### REACT-027 — A fragment has no host node **Difficulty:** Intermediate **Category:** Reconciliation **Question:** Returning `<>…` instead of a `
`: what is in the DOM? What fiber? Can React 18 put `onClick` or `ref` on the fragment? **Answer:** A fragment lets you return several elements without adding an extra DOM node. React still has an internal fiber for it, but there is no matching DOM element. The children go straight into the nearest real parent. That means no extra box to style and no element to attach a listener to. Swapping a fragment for a `
